skin_diseases.name: Acne
skin_diseases.description: A common skin condition characterized by pimples, blackheads, and whiteheads, usually on the face, chest, and shoulders. Occurs when hair follicles become plugged with oil and dead skin cells.

skin_diseases.name: Eczema
skin_diseases.description: A chronic inflammatory skin condition causing intense itching, redness, and dry, thickened skin. Often starts in childhood and may persist into adulthood. Associated with allergies and asthma.
symptoms: Small, raised bumps that may weep fluid

skin_diseases.name: Psoriasis
skin_diseases.description: A chronic autoimmune condition that causes rapid buildup of skin cells, leading to scaling on the skin's surface. Characterised by red, itchy, scaly patches. Often cyclic with flares and remissions.
causes: Autoimmune disorder (T-cells attack healthy skin cells)
symptoms: Red patches covered with thick, silvery scales
Dry, cracked skin that may bleed

skin_diseases.name: Urticaria
skin_diseases.description: Sudden appearance of raised, red, itchy welts (wheals) on the skin due to the release of histamine. Individual lesions typically resolve within 24 hours but new ones may appear. Can be acute (< 6 weeks) or chronic.
symptoms: Welts that vary in size and shape
treatments: Oral corticosteroids (for severe or prolonged attacks)

skin_diseases.name: Ringworm
skin_diseases.description: A common fungal infection of the skin presenting as a ring-shaped, scaly rash. Despite the name, it is not caused by a worm but by dermatophyte fungi. Highly contagious.
causes: Direct skin-to-skin contact with infected person or animal
Contact with contaminated surfaces or objects
symptoms: Ring-shaped rash with clear or scaly center
Hair loss in scalp ringworm (tinea capitis)
Nail changes in nail ringworm (tinea unguium)
treatments: Topical antifungals (clotrimazole, miconazole, terbinafine) for 2-4 weeks
Oral antifungals for scalp or nail infections (griseofulvin, itraconazole)
Selenium sulfide shampoo for scalp involvement

skin_diseases.name: Rosacea
skin_diseases.description: A chronic inflammatory skin condition primarily affecting the face, causing persistent redness, visible blood vessels, and sometimes acne-like bumps. More common in fair-skinned individuals, especially women aged 30-50.
causes: Environmental triggers: sun, wind, heat, spicy food, alcohol, stress
Certain medications and skin care products
symptoms: Thickened skin on nose (rhinophyma in severe cases)
treatments: Laser or light therapies (IPL) for redness/vessels
prevention: Protect face from wind and cold

skin_diseases.name: Contact Dermatitis
skin_diseases.description: Skin inflammation that occurs when skin comes into direct contact with a substance that causes irritation (irritant contact dermatitis) or an allergic reaction (allergic contact dermatitis). The rash is usually limited to the area of contact.
causes: Irritant contact: soaps, detergents, solvents, acids, bleach
Allergen contact: nickel (jewelry), poison ivy/oak, latex, fragrances, cosmetics, rubber
symptoms: Crusting and oozing in severe cases
treatments: Topical corticosteroids (hydrocortisone for mild, betamethasone for moderate-severe)
prevention: Wear protective gloves when handling irritants
Rinse skin immediately after irritant contact
affected_areas: Areas of direct contact with irritant

skin_diseases.name: Melasma
skin_diseases.description: A common skin condition causing symmetric patches of dark, discolored skin (hyperpigmentation) primarily on the face. More prevalent in women and people with darker skin tones. Often triggered or worsened by hormonal changes.
causes: Sun exposure (primary trigger — UV radiation stimulates melanin)
Hormonal changes (pregnancy, oral contraceptives, hormone therapy)
symptoms: Brown, tan, or blue-gray patches of skin
Symmetric distribution on both sides of face
Usually on cheeks, forehead, nose bridge, upper lip
No pain, itching, or physical discomfort

skin_diseases.name: Vitiligo
skin_diseases.description: A chronic skin condition in which the immune system destroys melanocytes (pigment-producing cells), resulting in smooth, white patches on the skin. Can affect any body part and may progressively spread. Affects about 1% of the global population.
symptoms: Flat, white or depigmented patches of skin
Patches that often start small and may enlarge
Commonly at body orifices (mouth, eyes, genitals)
Premature whitening/graying of hair, eyebrows, eyelashes
prevention: Sun protection with SPF 50+ (depigmented skin burns easily)
Screen for and treat associated thyroid disease

skin_diseases.name: Warts
skin_diseases.description: Small, rough, hard growths on the skin caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Common in children and young adults. Most resolve on their own but may take months to years. Many types exist, including common warts, plantar warts, and flat warts.
causes: Direct skin contact with infected person
Breaks or cuts in the skin allow viral entry
prevention: Avoid walking barefoot in public areas
Cover warts when in contact with others

skin_diseases.name: Seborrheic Dermatitis
skin_diseases.description: A common, chronic inflammatory skin condition affecting areas rich in sebaceous (oil) glands. Causes scaly patches, red skin, and stubborn dandruff. Affects the scalp most commonly but also occurs on the face and other areas.
causes: Malassezia yeast overgrowth (normally present on skin)
symptoms: White or yellowish greasy scales on skin
Crusty scales on scalp, ears, face, chest
treatments: Medicated shampoos (ketoconazole, selenium sulfide, zinc pyrithione)
prevention: Use medicated shampoo routinely if prone

skin_diseases.name: Cellulitis
skin_diseases.description: A serious bacterial skin infection that affects the deeper layers of the skin (dermis and subcutaneous tissue). Appears as a red, swollen, tender area that may spread rapidly. Requires prompt medical treatment.
causes: Bacteria entering through breaks in skin (Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus most common)
Skin injuries, cuts, insect bites, surgical wounds
Athlete's foot creating portal for bacteria
symptoms: Red streaks extending from area (sign of spreading)
treatments: IV antibiotics for severe or rapidly spreading infections
Marking border with pen to monitor spread
prevention: Treat athlete's foot and fungal infections

skin_diseases.name: Impetigo
skin_diseases.description: A highly contagious superficial bacterial skin infection, most common in young children. Characterized by honey-colored crusts over sores on the face, neck, and hands. Spreads easily by touch, towels, and clothing.
symptoms: Red sores that quickly rupture, ooze, and form honey-colored crusts
Can appear anywhere on body — face and hands most common
treatments: Topical antibiotics (mupirocin or fusidic acid ointment) for localized disease
Oral antibiotics (cefalexin, flucloxacillin, or clindamycin for extensive disease)
Gentle cleaning with warm soapy water
prevention: Do not share towels or personal items
Keep children home from school until crusts are healed or 48h after starting antibiotics

skin_diseases.name: Herpes Simplex
skin_diseases.description: A viral infection causing recurring blisters or sores. HSV-1 typically causes oral herpes (cold sores) and HSV-2 causes genital herpes, though either type can infect either area. The virus remains dormant in nerve cells and can reactivate.
causes: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) — primarily oral
Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) — primarily genital
Transmission through direct contact with sores, saliva, or genital secretions
Reactivation triggered by stress, illness, UV light, menstruation, immune suppression
symptoms: Tingling, burning, or itching before outbreak
Small, painful blisters that burst and crust over
Flu-like symptoms in primary infection (fever, lymph node swelling)
Cold sores on or around lips
treatments: Antiviral medications: acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir (shorten outbreaks)
prevention: Use condoms (reduce but don't eliminate transmission risk)
Avoid kissing when cold sore is active

skin_diseases.name: Chickenpox
skin_diseases.description: A highly contagious viral illness caused by varicella-zoster virus (VZV), characterized by an itchy rash with fluid-filled blisters. Common in children but can affect adults with more severe outcomes. After recovery, virus remains dormant and can reactivate as shingles in later life.
causes: Direct contact with rash of infected person
Airborne droplets from coughing or sneezing
Not immune (no prior infection or vaccination)
symptoms: Itchy rash starting on chest, back, face
Rash evolves: red spots → fluid-filled blisters → scabs
All three stages of rash may be present simultaneously
treatments: Paracetamol for fever (NOT aspirin — Reye's syndrome risk)
Antiviral acyclovir (for adults, immunocompromised, severe cases)
Trim nails to prevent scratching and secondary infection
prevention: Isolate infected individuals until all blisters scab over (typically 5-7 days after rash onset)
